shortAnswer: Estrogen is a group of hormones that lead puberty in most girls. The ovaries make most of it, and it helps shape the body’s changes and, later, the monthly cycle. Boys’ bodies make a little too. In the crew, Estra is the picture of that job: what a body does, never a measurement of your child.
kidVersion: Estra is the part of puberty that helps many girls’ bodies change: breasts start to grow, hips get rounder, and a few years later periods begin. Everyone’s body changes on its own schedule, and nobody’s is a race. If you ever have a question about your body, you can ask me, and I won’t make it weird.
whenToTalk: Talk with your pediatrician if signs of puberty start before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys, or if there are none by age 13 in girls or 14 in boys (the NHS draws its “delayed” line at 15 for everyone). Also check in if your child seems very upset about body changes. Anything between those ages is a wide, normal range.
safety: Hormones are not something to “boost” or “balance” with supplements, creams or special diets, and we don’t suggest any. If a product or an influencer promises to fix your child’s hormones, ask your pediatrician first.
explanation:
## What is estrogen, and what does it do in puberty?

Estrogen is a group of hormones, the chemical messages a body sends through the blood. In girls, the ovaries make most of it. Boys’ bodies make small amounts too, and part of a boy’s testosterone is converted into estrogen.

In the crew, **Estra** stands for the hormone that leads puberty in most girls. She is a picture of what a body does, not a measurement of your child. We never guess a hormone level from a mood, a pimple or a growth spurt, and nobody can read one from the outside.

What does she help with? The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says rising estrogen causes fat to settle in the hips and breasts, so a rounder shape is part of the plan, not a problem to fix. It also causes the clear or white vaginal fluid that many girls notice about 6 to 12 months before a first period. Later, with her partner Progi, she helps set up the monthly rhythm that Ciklo stands for.

## Who tells Estra when to start?

She doesn’t switch on by herself. NICHD, the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, explains that puberty’s trigger sits in a small part of the brain called the hypothalamus. It releases a signal called GnRH, which tells the pituitary gland to release two more hormones, LH and FSH. Those travel through the blood and signal the ovaries or testes to make sex hormones, including estrogens and testosterone.

In crew language, Elfi carries that message, and Gona, the ovaries and testes, makes Estra, Progi and Teo. Teo is the testosterone character, and he has his own page.

## What is normal, and when does it happen?

NICHD says puberty typically starts between ages 8 and 13 for girls and 9 and 14 for boys. That is a wide window on purpose. A girl who starts at 8 and a girl who starts at 13 can both be right where they should be.

The AAP says the earliest sign in most girls is breast “buds,” nickel-sized bumps under the nipple. In about 15% of girls, pubic hair comes first. The fastest growth in height usually happens between the start of breast budding and about six months before the first period, then it slows. Most girls get their first period within 2 to 3 years after breast buds appear, and the average age in the US is around 12.

Boys get a little Estra too. The AAP says three in four boys, if not more, have some breast growth during puberty, because some of their testosterone converts to estrogen, and it usually goes away in one to two years. Tell your son before he wonders. Many boys are relieved to hear it.

## Does estrogen make girls moody?

No. It is tempting to say “it’s her hormones,” but a hormone’s name doesn’t explain a slammed door. The National Institute of Mental Health notes that many teens don’t get enough sleep, which makes it harder to pay attention and control impulses, and that the sleep hormone melatonin works differently in teens. Friends matter more. And the prefrontal cortex, the planning-and-braking region Fronti runs, is one of the last parts of the brain to mature.

Some girls do feel tired or sore in the days before a period. That is common, and it is real. But it is a few days in a month, not a personality. Sleep, stress, friends and a brain still under construction are the better places to look first. Calling a daughter “hormonal” can also end the very conversation she needed.

## What helps at home?

Habits, not products. Protect sleep with a steady wake-up time and phones that charge outside the bedroom. Get daylight and movement she actually enjoys. Serve regular meals of real food, and keep diet talk out of it, because a changing shape is a normal part of puberty.

Keep talking. The AAP says talking about puberty should not be a one-time discussion, and that small conversations keep the door open. Think a hundred small talks, not one big one, ideally side by side in the car or while cooking. The AAP suggests starting around the breast bud stage, before the changes are all done. Boys need the real words too: what Estra does in girls’ bodies, and a little in theirs.

Estra doesn’t need boosting, balancing or fixing. If you are unsure whether your child’s timing is typical, bring the question to your pediatrician, who can look at the whole picture. Nobody’s timing is a race.
whatToSay:
Instead of: “Why is your body changing so early? That’s weird.” | Say: “Bodies start puberty at different ages, and yours is doing exactly what bodies do. Nothing’s wrong, and I’m here if you want to talk.” | Why: Typical puberty spans ages 8 to 13 in girls, and teasing about timing turns a normal change into shame.

Instead of: “You’ll understand when you’re older.” | Say: “Let’s talk about what’s happening in your body now. Ask me anything, and I’ll tell you the truth.” | Why: The AAP suggests talking early and often, in small conversations, starting around the breast bud stage.

Instead of: “It’s just your hormones.” | Say: “You’ve got a lot going on. Do you want to talk, or do you want company and a snack?” | Why: A hormone’s name doesn’t explain a hard day, and “hormonal” tends to end the conversation instead of opening it.

Instead of: “Maybe skip dessert, you’re filling out.” | Say: “Bodies get rounder and taller in puberty. That’s normal. Let’s keep eating regular meals and doing things that feel good.” | Why: A rounder shape is a normal part of puberty, and diet talk can plant body shame that lasts.

Instead of: “That’s girl stuff, so you don’t need to know.” | Say: “Girls’ bodies make a hormone called estrogen in puberty, and boys’ bodies make a little too. Ask me anything.” | Why: If your son asks, boys and girls both get the real words, and a boy who knows is a kinder brother and friend.

Instead of: “Your friend is already developing, what’s wrong with you?” | Say: “Everyone’s timing is different, and it’s not a race. If you’re ever worried, we can ask the doctor together.” | Why: Nobody’s timing is a race, and the typical window is wide on purpose.
